children: By Anoop Menon

French engineering and technology company Technip Energies said access through the Strait of Hormuz for transporting large equipment will become increasingly critical to the execution of some Middle East projects in 2027, even as it reported stable regional operations and contained financial impacts from ongoing disruptions.

CEO Arnaud Pieton said alternative logistics routes had allowed the company to maintain progress on projects, although transporting critical equipment remained a challenge due to weight and height restrictions on overland routes.

“Looking ahead to 2027, access through the Strait of Hormuz for large equipment will become increasingly important for sustaining execution on a small number of projects,” he said during the company's nine-month results conference call on Thursday.

Pieton said additional costs were primarily related to first, logistics constraints related to alternative shipping routes, standby fees, equipment storage at marshalling yards and second, the resequencing of construction activities due to these constraints, with the associated impact on operational efficiency.

However, the rate at which incremental costs were being incurred remained contained and in line with recent trends, he said, noting that ongoing commercial discussions with clients were progressing towards resolving cost-related claims.
“The situation is currently stable, with good operational progress translating into solid cash generation,” Pieton said.

Chief Financial Officer Bruno Vibert said recurring earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) in the Project Delivery segment fell 33 percent year-on-year to €218.5 million ($244 million) in the first nine months of 2026, with the margin declining to 5.2 percent from 8 percent.
The decline reflected additional logistics and productivity costs on certain Middle East projects, alongside the assessment of disputed items recorded in the first half, he said.
Vibert said the company was pursuing its contractual rights to recover these costs, although the amount and timing of any recoveries remained subject to ongoing commercial negotiations.

On Wednesday, US-based oilfield services company Baker Hughes said it expects activity in the Middle East to decline in the fourth quarter, returning broadly to second-quarter levels due to higher logistics costs and supply chain challenges.
Order backlog rises to $27bln

Technip Energies reported a more than fourfold increase in adjusted order intake to €14.1 billion ($15.7 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, compared with €3.36 billion ($3.8 billion) a year earlier.
Its adjusted order backlog reached €24.51 billion ($27 billion) at the end of September, up 46 percent from €16.76 billion ($19 billion) a year earlier.
Pieton said year-to-date order intake was nearly 75 percent higher than the company's average annual order intake since 2023, strengthening its medium-term revenue outlook.

Group revenue increased 3 percent to €5.60 billion ($6.27 billion) from €5.42 billion ($6.06 billion) in the corresponding period of 2025 driven by Project Delivery, while adjusted recurring EBITDA declined 20 percent to €384.7 million ($430.4 million) from €478 million ($535 million) mainly due operating conditions experienced in the Middle East in the second quarter.
The recurring EBITDA margin narrowed to 6.9 percent from 8.8 percent.
Adjusted net profit attributable to the group fell 34 percent to €184.8 million ($206.75 million) from €281.9 million ($315.38 million).
Despite the earnings pressure, Technip Energies maintained its 2026 guidance and said it remained on track to generate more than €800 million ($895 million) in annual EBITDA by 2028.
(Writing by Anoop Menon; Editing by SA Kader)
